Clairaut’s equation.

DEFINITION 1. Differential equation
                                        y = xy ′ + ϕ(y ′)                                        (1)

is called Clairaut’s equation.
We see that DE (1) is linear in both x and y, but it is not explicit with respect to y ′. Using the change
y ′(x) = p(x), (1) reads
                                        y = xp + ϕ(p).                                         (2)

Differentiating this equation with respect to x, we obtain

                                 p = p + xp′ + ϕ′(p)p′,

whence
                                           p′(x + ϕ′(p)) = 0.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 10, 2026                 3 / 49

If p′ = 0, then p = C, where C are arbitrary constants. Introducing this in (2), we get the general
solution of Clairaut’s equation
                                        y = Cx + ϕ(C).                                        (3)

The second possibility, x = −ϕ′(p), yields the singular solution, expressed in parametric form

                               x = −ϕ′(p),   y = −pϕ′(p) + ϕ(p).

Indeed, this solution cannot be obtained from the general one by giving particular value to C.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 10, 2026                 4 / 49

EXAMPLE 1
Find the general solution of Clairaut’s equation

                                       y = xy ′ + exp(y ′).                                       (4)


To solve this equation, we introduce the substitution p(x) = y ′(x), which transforms (4) into

                                       y = xp + exp(p).                                        (5)

Differentiating this relation with respect to x and using the fact that p is a function of x, we obtain

                                p = p + xp′ + exp(p)p′,

so that after cancellation,
                                             p′ x + exp(p) = 0.

This factored form gives two distinct possibilities. The first arises when p′ = 0, which means p = C for
some arbitrary constant C. Substituting this back into (5) yields the general solution of Clairaut’s
equation,
                                       y = Cx + exp(C).



Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 10, 2026                 5 / 49

This family of straight lines represents the general solution, parameterized by the constant C.
The second possibility comes from setting the other factor to zero, namely x + exp(p) = 0, which gives
x = −exp(p). Substituting this into (5) leads to the singular solution, expressed in parametric form as

                    x = −exp(p),     y = −p exp(p) + exp(p) = exp(p)(1 −p),

where p serves as the parameter.
To obtain an explicit representation, we eliminate the parameter p by noting that p = ln(−x).
Substituting this into the expression for y yields the singular solution in explicit form,

                                      y = −x 1 −ln(−x) .

This singular solution is not contained in the general family y = Cx + exp(C) for any finite value of C.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 10, 2026                 6 / 49

EXAMPLE 2
Solve the initial value problem for Clairaut’s equation

                                y = xy ′ + (y ′)3 −3y ′,   y(0) = 0.

 We consider Clairaut’s equation with cubic nonlinearity

                                     y = xy ′ + (y ′)3 −3y ′.

Here ϕ(p) = p3 −3p. The function ϕ(p) attains a local maximum at p = −1 with value 2, and a local
minimum at p = 1 with value −2.
Introduce the substitution p = y ′. The equation becomes

                                       y = xp + p3 −3p.

Differentiate this relation with respect to x:

                               p = p + xp′ + (3p2 −3)p′.

After canceling p, we obtain
                                            p′ x + 3p2 −3 = 0.

This factored form yields two distinct possibilities.
The first possibility is p′ = 0, which gives p = C, where C is an arbitrary constant. Substituting this
back yields the general solution:
                                      y = Cx + C 3 −3C.

The second possibility is x + 3p2 −3 = 0, hence

                                         x = 3 −3p2.

Substituting x = 3 −3p2 into the expression for y, we get

                        y = xp + p3 −3p = p(3 −3p2) + p3 −3p = −2p3.

Thus the singular solution is given parametrically by

                                  x = 3 −3p2,     y = −2p3.

Eliminating the parameter p, we obtain the explicit form

Lagrange’s equation.

DEFINITION 2. Differential equation

                               A(y ′)y + B(y ′)x + C(y ′) = 0                                 (6)

is called Lagrange’s equation.
Supposing that A(y ′) ̸= 0, we divide by it and thus (6) reads

                                      y = ϕ(y ′)x + ψ(y ′).                                      (7)

Sometimes DE (7) is called Lagrange’s equation. We see that, in fact, Lagrange’s equation is a
generalization of Clairaut’s equation (ϕ(y ′) = y ′). The method of solving (7) is the same: we use the
change y ′(x) = p(x), thus getting
                                       y = ϕ(p)x + ψ(p),                                       (8)

then we differentiate this, and, taking into account that y ′ = p, we deduce





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 10, 2026                11 / 49

p = xϕ′(p)p′ + ϕ(p) + ψ′(p)p′

or
                               [ϕ(p) −p] + [xϕ′(p) + ψ′(p)]dp = 0.                              (9)
                                                      dx
If ϕ(p) is a constant, then (9) is an DE with separable variables.  If ϕ(p) is not constant and ϕ(p) ̸= p,
then (9) may be written in the form

              dx                   [ϕ(p) −p] + [xϕ′(p) + ψ′(p)] = 0 ⇒dx +  ϕ′(p)  x =  ψ′(p)              dp                               dp   ϕ(p) −p    p −ϕ(p),

which is a first order linear nonhomogeneous ODE, that can be solved by using the method described in
Lecture 4. We get x as a function of p

                                       x = α(p)C + β(p)

with C an arbitrary constant. Getting back to (8), we deduce





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 10, 2026                12 / 49

y = ϕ(p)[α(p)C + β(p)] + ψ(p),

so that the general solution of Lagrange’s equation, written in parametric form, is

                      x = α(p)C + β(p),   y = ϕ(p)[α(p)C + β(p)] + ψ(p).

Now we suppose that for some value pi
                                             ϕ(pi) = pi.                                        (10)

Then p(x) ≡pi is the solution of DE (9) and we find from (8) and (10)

                           y = ϕ(pi)x + ψ(pi)   or   y = xpi + ψ(pi),

also representing solution of Lagrange’s equation.
